analysis.one_liner: Requires groups spending on elections to disclose their big donors and tightens the ban on foreign election money.
analysis.headline: The DISCLOSE Act, introduced by the Senate's Democratic leader and placed on the Senate calendar, never received a vote and ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force corporations, labor unions, Super PACs, and tax-exempt "dark money" groups to tell the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours whenever they spend more than $10,000 on election activity, and to name anyone who gives them $10,000 or more for politics. It would also close loopholes that let foreign money reach U.S. elections — including through shell companies, digital ads, ballot initiatives, and ads about judicial nominees — and make it a crime punishable by up to five years in prison to set up a company to hide foreign election spending. It never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would be able to see who is paying for the political ads they watch: any covered organization spending more than $10,000 in an election cycle would have to file a report with the FEC within 24 hours listing each disbursement over $1,000 and identifying every funder who gave $10,000 or more, plus the "beneficial owners" of shell entities doing the spending [S2][S3]. Voters would also gain from tighter foreign-money rules: a ban on foreign nationals participating in spending decisions, an expansion of the ban to paid digital ads and judicial-nomination ads, a prohibition on foreign money in ballot-initiative campaigns, a requirement that CEOs certify under penalty of perjury that no foreign national directed the spending, and a new five-year prison penalty for using a company to conceal foreign contributions [S2][S3]. After each election cycle the FEC would have to audit how much illicit foreign money entered the race and report to Congress [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting to know who funds campaign ads

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations — corporations, labor organizations, 501(c) groups, and Super PACs — must report to the FEC within 24 hours of crossing $10,000 in campaign spending, naming each disbursement over $1,000, the candidate involved, and every person who paid $10,000 or more into the effort.

Entities making campaign spending must disclose their 'beneficial owners' — the real people who control them or profit from them — with anti-abuse rules aimed at nominees, intermediaries, and layered legal entities.

The foreign-money ban is extended to disbursements for paid web and digital ads, communications supporting or attacking judicial nominations, ballot initiatives and referenda, and payments to internet influencers; foreign nationals are barred from directing or participating in spending decisions, and corporate political funds must certify that foreign directors abstain.

Creating or using a company with the intent to conceal foreign election money becomes a federal crime carrying up to five years in prison, and CEOs must certify under penalty of perjury each year that no foreign national directed their political spending.

The FEC must audit each federal election cycle for illicit foreign money and report to Congress, including analysis of foreign-funded disinformation aimed at depressing turnout among rural, Black, minority, military, and veteran communities.

analysis.who_pays: The groups that spend big on elections: Super PACs, corporate political programs, labor unions, and tax-exempt nonprofits that currently fund ads without naming their funders. They would face 24-hour reporting deadlines, perjury-certification requirements by their top officers, and the loss of donor anonymity for anyone giving $10,000 or more toward political spending [S3]. Large online platforms (50 million or more monthly U.S. users) that sell political ads would bear new responsibilities around covered advertising, and companies handling political money would face audit exposure from mandatory FEC reviews of foreign money [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Super PACs, corporations, unions, dark-money nonprofits

drawbacks.text: The compliance load is heavy: groups must file within 24 hours of crossing the $10,000 threshold, and a chief executive must personally certify under penalty of perjury that foreign nationals did not influence spending decisions and that spending was not coordinated with candidates — exposure that falls hardest on organizations without large legal and compliance staffs.

Critics argue the bill was designed for a legal landscape that no longer matches it: it funnels constitutional challenges to a single court (the D.C. district court), lets members of Congress intervene, and includes a severability clause — all provisions that anticipate court challenges to mandatory donor disclosure under First Amendment case law.

The bill's own exceptions show its limits: news outlets and their online platforms are excluded from the definitions, and anyone facing 'serious threats, harassment, or reprisals' can have their name withheld — carve-outs that both protect critics and leave disclosure uneven.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — voters seeing who pays for the ads aimed at them — is real and reaches the money that currently moves through Super PACs and shell nonprofits invisibly. The costs are genuine but narrower than the benefit: reporting deadlines and perjury certifications for organizations that choose to spend on elections, and the loss of anonymity only for funders above $10,000. The bigger risk is not the compliance burden but whether courts would uphold mandatory donor disclosure; the bill's own structure — special judicial-review rules and a severability clause — reads as preparation for that fight.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was placed on the Senate calendar the day after it was introduced and was never called up for a vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended, with no cosponsors and no committee action.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Schumer introduced S. 2671, the DISCLOSE Act of 2021, in the Senate on August 6, 2021.
The bill was read twice in two days and placed directly on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 120) on August 7, 2021 — skipping committee referral entirely.
No senator cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero.
After being placed on the calendar, the bill received no further action — no debate, no roll-call vote — and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The organizations that spend large sums on elections without naming their funders — Super PACs, corporate political programs, and dark-money nonprofits — are better off, because donor secrecy survived and the foreign-money loopholes the bill targeted remain open.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it read twice and placed directly on the Senate calendar within two days, bypassing committee referral.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the bill never received floor time in the Republican-relevant sense — it sat on the calendar untouched for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken, but the partisan shape is stark: the Senate's top Democrat introduced it alone and not one of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on.

industries.industry: Super PACs and dark-money nonprofits (501(c) groups)
industries.note: These groups exist to move large sums into elections, often without naming funders. The bill would force 24-hour disclosure of every $10,000-plus funder and of the real people behind shell entities, eliminating the donor secrecy that is their core product.

Corporations would lose the ability to fund election activity anonymously and would have to certify annually, under penalty of perjury, that foreign nationals did not direct their political money — a compliance cost and a transparency loss for shareholders' and managers' political influence.

Labor organizations are covered organizations under the bill and face the same 24-hour reporting and funder disclosure as corporations, though money flowing in through member dues is treated differently — unions gain the same transparency rules applying to their corporate adversaries but lose some spending discretion.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and digital ad networks
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users, and third-party ad vendors at that scale, would face new definitions and restrictions around qualified political advertising, including the foreign-money ban applied to paid digital promotion — an administrative burden, but one aimed at money, not at platforms' general business.

The bill explicitly exempts news stories, commentary, editorials, and platforms owned by broadcasting stations, newspapers, and magazines from its definitions — a carve-out that leaves traditional media outside the new disclosure machinery while digital political spending is regulated.
